title: "Salt-sensitive" essential hypertension in men. Is the sodium ion alone important?
authors: Kurtz TW, Al-Bander HA, Morris RC Jr
population: Five men with essential hypertension whose blood pressure was normal with dietary sodium chloride restricted to 10 mmol per day
funder: Supported by the General Clinical Research Center, University of California, San Francisco, with funds provided by grants (RR-00079, RO1-AM-32631 and RO1-HL-37696) from the National Institutes of Health, generous gifts from the Church and Dwight Corporation and the Emil Mosbacher, Jr., Foundation, and grants from the National Dairy Board administered in cooperation with the National Dairy Council and the Research Evaluation and Allocation Committee of the University of California, San Francisco. Dr. Kurtz is the recipient of a Public Health Service Clinical Investigator Award (HL-01490) from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
result: Sodium chloride 240 mmol per day (5.52 g sodium) for 7 days raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 16 ± 2 and 8 ± 2 mm Hg (mean ± SEM, P < 0.05); an equimolar amount of sodium as sodium citrate induced no change, and replacing supplemental sodium chloride with sodium citrate abolished the rise. Both salts induced comparable sodium retention, weight gain and suppression of plasma renin activity and aldosterone; sodium chloride, but not sodium citrate, increased plasma volume and urinary calcium excretion. The authors call the findings preliminary and state that they require confirmation in larger numbers of patients of both sexes.
